source.title: Transformers Struggle to Learn to Search
source.authors: Abulhair Saparov; S. Pawar; Shreyas Pimpalgaonkar; Nitish Joshi; Richard Yuanzhe Pang; Vishakh Padmakumar; Seyed Mehran Kazemi; Najoung Kim; He He

record.tranche_reason: The study varies transformer size and reports held-out task loss in several synthetic search-training settings, a different task and setup from language-model pretraining scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work in related work but reports no results from those studies. Loss sweeps over input graph size are not rows for the listed versions because graph size is not parameter count, training tokens, or compute; the paper describes these sweeps in Figures 6, 9, 11, 14, and 16 as showing greater difficulty on larger graphs. The scaling-loss rows below concern model-size sweeps. The paper does not fit power laws or estimate exponents.
record.test_reason: The paper trains small transformers from scratch on synthetic graph-search tasks and asks whether larger models learn search more easily. It reports qualitative readings of loss curves, not a fitted or checkable power-law relation of loss in parameters, data or compute. That is a related but different construct: whether an algorithmic capability is acquired, read from training dynamics. Scaling-law work is cited only in related work. The model-size sweeps are therefore recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: transformers can learn search given a balanced training distribution, using a path-merging algorithm. Difficulty grows with input graph size, and larger models do not resolve it, even with DFS or selection-inference intermediate steps. The authors allow that much larger models or other training methods might differ.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains small transformers from scratch on generated graph-search tasks and reports loss curves, rather than fitting language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports substantial dependence on training distribution for search accuracy. Its scale results also vary by task and architecture setting: graph search, depth-first search, selection-inference, and decoder-only models with rotary embeddings are evaluated separately.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic graph search, DFS and selection-inference tasks, increasing model size (about 0.4M–60M non-embedding parameters) does not make learning the task easier. Larger models escape an early plateau sooner or need fewer examples, but need more FLOPs, and show no pattern in reaching the global loss minimum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For algorithmic search tasks trained from scratch, increasing transformer size does not reliably reduce the data or compute needed to acquire the algorithm.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimum test loss and the fraction of seeds that converge worsen sharply as maximum input graph size grows, at fixed model size (Fig. 6, 10, 11, 14, 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learnability of search by transformers degrades with problem (graph) size at fixed model size.

record.problems: The experiments concern small synthetic-task transformers, not language-model pretraining. No power-law fitting or exponent estimates are reported. The loss values are presented in plots rather than numerical tables, and some conclusions aggregate results across seeds or model sizes.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted curve points and seed traces were not extracted. The graph-size sweeps and natural-language proof-search loss curves in Figures 6, 9, 11, 14, and 16 vary task difficulty rather than parameters, tokens, or compute, so they do not directly measure a listed version.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from fitted small runs.
No power-law fit in the synthetic search regime; model-size sweeps measure ease of learning search, not loss scaling form.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V5 limits_scope labels are not adopted. The study does not report power-law loss behaviour in any regime, and its model-size sweeps measure whether and how fast a synthetic capability is learned. Evidence is figure-only, with curves smoothed and reported as minimum over seeds.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fits to smaller runs are used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep between parameter count and token count.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study does not fit or test a power-law form or exponents. It tests synthetic search-task training, not other modalities, repeated-data pretraining, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No relationship between pretraining loss and downstream-task performance is tested.
No comparison of fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, or alternative power-law fits; no claim about disagreement between published exponents.

rows.subject: GPT-2-architecture transformers (model-size sweep; aggregate finding)
rows.operation_detail: Varied non-embedding parameter count and tracked training and held-out test loss on balanced-distribution graph search.
rows.measure: Held-out test loss over training examples
rows.note: The authors report that larger models reach a local minimum near loss 10^0 more quickly, but find no discernible relationship between model size and training needed to reach the global minimum. This is the paper's qualitative aggregate finding across the plotted model sizes.
rows.check: Measures time to escape a loss plateau (local minimum near 10^0) versus model size during training on a synthetic task. It is not a power-law loss relation in a training regime, and there is no fit and no tabulated values. 'Partial' against V5 cannot be read from this measure.

rows.subject: Decoder-only transformers with rotary positional embeddings (model-size sweep; aggregate finding)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and tracked training and held-out test loss against FLOPs on graph search.
rows.note: The authors state that increasing model scale does not help the model learn the task more easily; the plotted loss values are not tabulated.
rows.check: RoPE decoder-only model-size sweep (Fig. 12). The authors say scale 'does not help the model to learn the task more easily'. This is ease of learning, not a power-law form; the measure cannot show V5's effect.

rows.subject: Transformers trained on the depth-first-search task (model-size sweep; aggregate finding)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and tracked training and held-out test loss against training examples and FLOPs.
rows.measure: Held-out test loss against training examples and FLOPs
rows.locator: Figure 14; Section 6.1; Figure 14 caption in Section A.8
rows.note: The authors report that larger models can learn from fewer examples, but this advantage disappears when training cost is measured in FLOPs; larger models require more FLOPs to learn the task.
rows.check: DFS model-size sweep (Fig. 14, minimum over 15 seeds). Larger models need fewer examples but more FLOPs. This is a learning-efficiency observation without any power-law fit, so it is not a V5 measurement.

rows.subject: Transformers trained on the selection-inference task (model-size sweep; aggregate finding)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and tracked training and held-out test loss against FLOPs.

conditions.value: balanced distribution with frontier size 4 and branch count 4

rows.locator: Figure 17; Section 6.2; Figure 17 caption in Section A.11
rows.note: The authors state that increasing model scale does not help the model learn the task. The graph plots loss for several sizes; numerical values are not tabulated.
rows.check: Selection-inference model-size sweep (Fig. 17). The authors say scale does not help learn the task. No power-law fit; the plotted values cannot be read as a scaling-law test.
